title: A Portrait for the Visitor
premise: Rafael Kavanagh hosts a late-night call-in show in the fading town of Hollowmere, where the voices on his line belong to listeners who died days earlier — all of them connected to a 1974 disappearance the town buried along with its secrets. When an excavation crew unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside, Rafael discovers he is the last living heir of the family that locked it, and the dead are calling in their debts. To survive the frost that is slowly writing itself across his skin, he must uncover what was taken in 1974 — a child, a confession, and a ledger of names — and return each debt to its rightful owner. In the end Rafael broadcasts the truth live, gives himself to the door as payment for the town's survival, and becomes the newest voice calling in from the dark.
about_author: August Dunmore is the pen name of a former small-town radio producer who spent a decade collecting the strange calls that never made it to air. Dunmore writes horror rooted in municipal secrets, believing every town keeps one door it refuses to open.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. During his overnight shift at WLMR, a caller describes her own funeral from last Tuesday; Rafael checks the obituaries and confirms it. He keeps broadcasting anyway, counting the studio doors out of habit. The beat is quiet dread — the reader learns the rules of the show before Rafael admits them to himself.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Crews digging the new flood channel behind Kavanagh family land strike something: a steel door, rusted shut, sealed from the inside. Rafael arrives as the only living Kavanagh and feels frost bloom under his fingernails when he touches the frame. Beat: reluctant inheritance — the past has found him first.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Rafael and dispatcher Maren Oduya, who starts logging the impossible calls. Each dead listener mentions the same date — October 1974 — and asks Rafael questions only his grandfather could answer. Emotional beat: mounting unease as the pattern becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Kept
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, exploring the boarded Kavanagh house. He finds a hidden ledger listing nineteen names, nineteen payments received, and one entry torn out. Frost creeps up the walls wherever he lingers. Beat: guilt by bloodline; the house remembers him even if he doesn't remember it.

chapters.title: Maren's List
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. She cross-references callers against missing-persons files and finds they match children reported gone in '74 — alive until last week, then dead within days of the excavation starting. Beat: horror reframed as arithmetic; someone or something is finishing an old count.

chapters.title: The First Debt
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A caller named Ida demands he return 'the coat' — a child's winter coat Rafael finds folded in the cellar stairwell of the old house. When he lays it on the sealed door, the frost recedes an inch. Beat: tentative hope that debts can be paid, not just suffered.

chapters.title: Council of Silence
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs via a tense town meeting. Mayor Prentiss, whose father signed the 1974 order, pushes to concrete over the door. Old-timer Gus Whitlock nearly speaks, then doesn't. Rafael realizes the living are more invested in silence than the dead. Beat: institutional corruption versus individual conscience.

chapters.title: Frostwork
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The pattern on his skin now forms legible words — names, dates, a countdown. His doctor can't explain tissue cold enough to crack a thermometer. Beat: body horror as deadline; the frost is writing its final pattern and Rafael is the page.

chapters.title: Nineteen Voices
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter told through the radio calls themselves, each dead voice giving one fragment of the night in 1974: a party, a fire, a locked cellar, adults choosing who came out. Beat: devastating mosaic; the reader assembles the tragedy before Rafael does.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In the church archive he matches the ledger to baptismal records and identifies the torn-out name: a twentieth child, unlisted, uncounted — his own father, who survived because someone else paid his share. Beat: personal reckoning; Rafael's inheritance is a stolen life.

chapters.title: Prentiss's Bargain
chapters.summary: Mayor Prentiss's POV. He offers Rafael hush money and a demolition permit, revealing his family has been paying the door annually since '74 — with other people's children. Beat: power's corruption laid bare; the town's prosperity was always a subscription price.

chapters.title: Break-In
chapters.summary: Rafael and Maren break into the county records vault at night, pursued by someone they never quite see. They recover the original 1974 police report, suppressed, naming every adult who stood outside the cellar while it burned. Beat: thriller momentum; justice requires evidence, and evidence requires risk.

chapters.title: The Door Opens Inward
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The seal breaks — not outward but inward, as if opened from inside long ago. Cold air carries voices singing a skipping rhyme. Maren pulls him back before he steps through. Beat: threshold terror; the way in is also the way it wants him to go.

chapters.title: Confession on Air
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, live broadcast. He reads the suppressed report aloud, naming the families, including his own. Callers go silent, then one by one say 'received.' The frost stops spreading. Beat: catharsis through exposure; truth as the first currency the door accepts.

chapters.title: Retribution, Unlicensed
chapters.summary: Multi-POV aftermath. Named families face ruin — resignations, confessions, one suicide — all without a single arrest. Rafael grapples with whether he delivered justice or just relocated cruelty. Beat: moral vertigo; justice outside the law cuts both ways.

chapters.title: The Nineteenth Caller
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A final caller claims to be the child everyone thought died in '74 — alive, old, and furious that Rafael's broadcast ended her decades of anonymity and safety. Beat: complication; exposure harms as well as heals.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, descending into the cellar with the ledger, the report, and his grandfather's recorded confession. He learns the true taken thing wasn't a child but a choice — the town traded one life for permission to forget. Beat: revelation; the debt is memory itself.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The frost completes across his chest, spelling his own name beneath his grandfather's. Maren begs him to run; the door will accept a substitute debtor. Beat: sacrifice crystallizing; Rafael understands the exit costs exactly what he inherited.

chapters.title: Payment
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV at the threshold. He pays the debt with his grandfather's confession, the ledger, and finally his voice — surrendering his ability to speak above a whisper, the thing that made him a host. The door seals again, this time from the outside. Beat: climax and cost; survival priced in identity.

chapters.title: After the Frost
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Spring comes to Hollowmere. The excavation fills, the callers stop, and Rafael hosts his last show in near-silence, letting listeners hear the quiet instead. Beat: tender resolution; some prices buy peace rather than victory.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. On his final broadcast he reads the nineteen names aloud, then signs off with a whispered thank-you. As the transmitter dies, a new voice — young, unfamiliar — calls in asking for August Dunmore. Beat: haunting coda; the cycle finds its next teller.

chapters.title: A Portrait for the Visitor
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Maren's POV framed around a portrait hung in the station: Rafael painted from memory, frost still visible in his eyes. Visitors leave coins beneath it; none of the coins are ever there by morning. Beat: elegiac closure — the town remembers the only way it knows how, and the door stays fed.
